claims.text: The primary sector covers businesses that take growing materials or extractive output from the natural world - farming, fishing, forestry and mining; the secondary sector covers businesses that turn materials into finished goods by manufacturing or construction; the tertiary sector covers businesses that provide services rather than a physical product, such as transport, banking and retailing.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The classification of a business into primary, secondary or tertiary follows what its work actually does to materials, not what it sells: a bakery that mills its own flour straddles sectors, and the sector given is the one describing the main stage of its activity.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Examples place a business in its sector: a Karas lamb farm sits in the primary sector, an Ongwediva furniture maker in the secondary sector, and a Windhoek courier firm in the tertiary sector; a Chilean copper mine and a Norwegian fish cannery show the same basis at work in other economies.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Deindustrialisation is the long-run shift in the importance of business sectors, in which secondary-sector manufacturing tends to shrink as a share of an economy while tertiary services grow; industrialisation is the earlier shift in which manufacturing grows out of a mainly primary-sector economy.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: In developed economies the tertiary sector tends to be the largest because rising incomes let households spend a growing share on services, and because consumers expect services around the goods they buy.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: In many developing economies the primary sector tends to employ the most people because most households still depend on farming, fishing and extractive work, while mechanisation on farms pushes workers towards towns and service jobs over time.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: New manufacturing technology tends to shrink the share of work in secondary-sector factories, because machines and automation let each worker produce far more, so the same output needs fewer factory workers than before.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The private sector is the part of a mixed economy owned and controlled by individuals or companies, usually run for profit, while the public sector is the part owned and controlled by the state, usually run to provide services the population needs rather than to profit.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A mixed economy contains both a private sector and a public sector: in Namibia, Oshakati Premier Juice (a private juice processor) sits in the private sector, while NamWater, the state-owned water utility, sits in the public sector.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The main features that tell the sectors apart are ownership (private owners against the state), main aim (profit against providing a service), and control (private shareholders or owners against government ministers and officials).

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.
